prompt.context: Our client is a drug store chain, similar to CVS. They have been losing profits for the last few years.
prompt.question: Can you help us identify the reasons and means to improve the profits?

clarifying_info.q: What types of stores does the client operate?
clarifying_info.a: Stores are typical to CVS, located in several areas.

clarifying_info.q: What are the key business areas within each store?
clarifying_info.a: Stores have three key business areas: 1) Pharmacy, 2) Health and Beauty, 3) General Merchandise.

framework: Revenue: product mix trends, customer segment trends, pricing/discount trends, location mix
Costs: new stores, renovations, labor/overtime/turnover/training, new supplier contracts, logistics costs
Competition: new locations nearby, competitive pricing, product variety, integration of suppliers, online shopping

questions.prompt: After developing a framework, identify whether profitability differs by product type. Use the following data provided verbally: Pharmacy — $20,000 sales/sq ft, 5% profit margin; Health and Beauty — $10,000 sales/sq ft, 20% profit margin; General Merchandise — $5,000 sales/sq ft, 10% profit margin. Calculate profit per sq ft for each product type.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply sales/sq ft by profit margin for each product type to derive profit per sq ft. Identify which products are most and least profitable per unit of floor space.

math.setup: Profit per sq ft = Sales per sq ft × Profit margin
math.answer: Pharmacy: $1K/sq ft; Health and Beauty: $2K/sq ft; General Merchandise: $0.5K/sq ft. Health and Beauty is the most profitable per sq ft; General Merchandise is the least.

questions.prompt: Given that General Merchandise has low profit per sq ft, brainstorm ways the company could improve the cost structure of General Merchandise — using milk as a specific example. Structure your answer across the value chain.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure cost improvement ideas across Acquisition, Retail operations, and Distribution. A strong answer covers multiple levers under each bucket.

questions.prompt: You learn the following about store mix: 60% of stores are located near hospitals, in areas with heavy competition, or in high-crime areas — these stores make a 10% loss. The remaining 40% of stores make 25% profits. What do you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that loss-making stores should be closed, but also consider risks: product shift could change the 10% loss, loss of key customers focused on health and beauty, and backlash from closing stores. Candidate should also recommend leveraging lessons from profitable stores: identify common traits, assess opportunity for growth, evaluate competition and market size in those locations.

brainstorming.prompt: How could the company improve the cost structure of General Merchandise (e.g., milk)?

categories.name: Retail Operations
ideas: Improve demand forecasting to reduce inventory

recommendation: The client is losing profits due to three interconnected issues: an unfavorable product mix (over-reliance on low-margin General Merchandise), a poor store mix (60% of stores are loss-making at -10%), and suboptimal location decisions.

We recommend two priority actions: first, optimize product mix by reallocating floor space toward Health and Beauty (highest profit per sq ft at $2K) while reducing General Merchandise footprint; second, close or restructure the 60% of underperforming stores after a detailed location-by-location review.
risks: Closing stores may trigger supplier backlash and loss of key Health and Beauty customers in those locations
Reducing General Merchandise could eliminate foot traffic that drives higher-margin purchases
Product mix shift may not resolve the -10% loss if underlying cost structure remains unchanged
next_steps: Conduct a store-by-store profitability analysis to prioritize closures
Pilot a rebalanced floor layout with higher Health and Beauty allocation in profitable stores
Renegotiate supplier contracts for General Merchandise to improve margins before any full exit decision
Identify common traits of the profitable 40% of stores and use as a template for future site selection
